title: Leaderless Replication
explain: In leaderless replication every replica of a key can accept reads and writes, and nobody orders writes. Whichever node receives a request acts as that request's coordinator and talks to the key's replicas. It gives high availability and write throughput, in exchange for replicas that may disagree and need version metadata and repair.
model:
My mental model: every engineer can read and write, but each handles one customer request; every change ends up in the same shared service, and eventually everyone learns what happened.

Structure (Dynamo / Cassandra style):

```
Key ─hash─▶ Partition P ─replication factor N=3─▶ Replica set [A, B, C]
Client ─▶ any node = Coordinator (for this request only)
            ├─ write to replicas, wait for W acks
            ├─ read replicas, wait for R responses
            └─ reconcile versions
```

- A write succeeds when **W** replicas confirm; a read consults **R** and reconciles. Details: [write path](#/sd/f/leaderless-write-path), [read path](#/sd/f/leaderless-read-path), [quorum](#/sd/f/leaderless-quorum), [repair](#/sd/f/leaderless-repair).
- **No failover:** a down replica just means fewer acks.
- **Costs:** replicas may disagree so every value needs version metadata; concurrent writes can conflict; no global order or cross-key transaction.

**Use** for high availability and write throughput on key-addressed data that tolerates eventual convergence (carts, sessions, time series, feeds). **Avoid** where an invariant needs a single arbiter (balances, uniqueness) unless you add consensus. Contrast [leader-based replication](#/sd/f/leader-based-replication).

details.q: What does a client see when one of three replicas dies, at W = 2?
details.a: Nothing: two live replicas still ack and the write succeeds. In single-leader, losing the leader blocks writes until failover completes. That is the availability advantage.

details.q: What is a coordinator, and why is it not a leader?
details.a: The node that happened to receive a request and fans it out to the replicas. It has no authority over other requests and no ordering role: two coordinators handling the same key concurrently is normal.

details.q: Two coordinators write the same key at the same time. What is true?
details.a: Both proceed independently; replicas may receive them in different orders. Resolution depends on version metadata (LWW timestamps or version vectors), not arrival order.

details.q: How much disk does a cluster need?
details.a: Unique data times the replication factor, divided by nodes. 30 TB across 9 nodes with N = 3 is 90 TB of total storage, so 10 TB per node on average.

details.q: Which workloads fit and which do not?
details.a: Fit: carts, sessions, time-series, activity feeds, anything key-addressed and convergence-tolerant. Don't fit: balances, uniqueness constraints, inventory of the last item, anything that needs a single arbiter.

details.q: What do you give up compared with leader-based?
details.a: A single history: replicas can disagree, concurrent writes can conflict, there is no multi-key transaction, and reads are only fresh if the quorum overlap holds and repair keeps up.

prompts.q: Explain leaderless replication and the role of a coordinator.
points: Any replica can accept reads and writes
Coordinator is per request, not a leader
Waits for W acks or R responses

prompts.q: Compare leaderless with leader-based and say when you would pick each.
points: Leaderless: availability, no failover, write throughput
Leaderless needs version metadata and repair
Balances/uniqueness need a leader or consensus
Carts, sessions, time series suit leaderless

prompts.q: Trace a request through a leaderless cluster from client to replicas.
points: Hash gives partition, partition gives replica set
That node coordinates with the replicas
